lessons.title: Reading a medicine label
lessons.description: The active ingredient is the substance that produces a medicine's effect.
objectives: Explain reading a medicine label in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: The active ingredient is the substance that produces a medicine's effect. The Drug Facts panel on an over-the-counter product lists the ingredient and its amount.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: The uses section describes what the product treats. Warnings explain situations that need extra care. Directions describe how to use that specific product.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: Read the label each time. Check active ingredients before combining products so that you do not accidentally take the same ingredient twice.

lessons.title: Brand and generic medicines
lessons.description: A brand name is a product name.
objectives: Explain brand and generic medicines in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: A brand name is a product name. A generic name identifies its active ingredient. One ingredient can be sold under several brand names.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: FDA-approved generic medicines must match their brand counterparts in active ingredient, strength, dosage form, route, and expected clinical benefit.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: Packaging, color, and some inactive ingredients can differ. Ask your pharmacist to explain a change in appearance or whether two products are equivalent.

lessons.title: Understanding what medicines do
lessons.description: Medicines can prevent or treat illness and help control symptoms.
objectives: Explain understanding what medicines do in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: Medicines can prevent or treat illness and help control symptoms. Some are used regularly; others are used for a short time or for a specific situation.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: Every medicine has possible benefits and risks. Other medicines, alcohol, foods, or pregnancy may affect whether a medicine is suitable for someone.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: Learn why each medicine was prescribed and how to use it. Your own instructions come from your prescriber and pharmacist, rather than a general educational summary.

lessons.title: Side effects and allergies
lessons.description: A side effect is an unwanted effect of a medicine.
objectives: Explain side effects and allergies in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: A side effect is an unwanted effect of a medicine. An allergic reaction involves the immune system. These are different kinds of medicine reactions.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: Not everyone gets the same reaction. Keep track of what happened, which product you took, and when symptoms started so your care team can assess it.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: Tell your pharmacist or clinician about suspected reactions. Trouble breathing or swelling of the face or throat needs emergency medical attention.

lessons.title: What antibiotics can and cannot treat
lessons.description: Antibiotics act against bacteria.
objectives: Explain what antibiotics can and cannot treat in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: Antibiotics act against bacteria. They do not treat viruses such as those causing colds or flu. A clinician decides when an antibiotic is needed.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: Antibiotic resistance occurs when bacteria change so a medicine no longer works well against them. Unnecessary antibiotic use contributes to this problem.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: Follow the prescribed instructions and discuss side effects with your clinician. Do not share antibiotics, use someone else's prescription, or keep leftovers for a future illness.

lessons.title: Understanding medicine interactions
lessons.description: An interaction happens when another substance or health condition changes a medicine's effects.
objectives: Explain understanding medicine interactions in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: An interaction happens when another substance or health condition changes a medicine's effects. It may increase unwanted effects or reduce the intended benefit.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: Prescription medicines can interact with nonprescription products, supplements, foods, or alcohol. A product sold without a prescription can still cause an interaction.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: Give your pharmacist a complete list of what you take. Read warnings and ask before adding a new product rather than trying to judge combinations yourself.

lessons.title: Keeping medicines organized
lessons.description: A medicine list records product names, amounts, and the times you use them.
objectives: Explain keeping medicines organized in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: A medicine list records product names, amounts, and the times you use them. Keeping one current list helps you and your care team understand your routine.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: A written schedule, appropriate organizer, or reminder can help you remember a planned dose. Ask a pharmacist whether your medicines are suitable for an organizer.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: Record a dose only after taking it. If you miss one, check the medicine's instructions or ask your pharmacist instead of guessing how to catch up.

lessons.title: Storing medicines safely
lessons.description: Heat, light, air, and moisture can damage medicines.
objectives: Explain storing medicines safely in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: Heat, light, air, and moisture can damage medicines. A bathroom may be too damp or warm even if it has a medicine cabinet.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: Read storage instructions for each product. Some medicines require special temperatures. Keep products in their original containers unless a pharmacist advises otherwise.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: Keep medicines away from children and pets. Check expiry dates and ask a pharmacist about products that look or smell different or were stored incorrectly.

lessons.title: Disposing of unused medicines
lessons.description: Unwanted or expired medicines can be taken by accident or misused.
objectives: Explain disposing of unused medicines in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: Unwanted or expired medicines can be taken by accident or misused. Safe disposal matters when a treatment ends or a prescription changes.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: A medicine take-back service is usually the preferred disposal option. Your pharmacist or local waste service can help you find an appropriate collection program.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: Do not routinely flush medicines. Only specific products have instructions allowing this. Follow current product and local disposal instructions, and remove personal information from discarded packaging.

lessons.title: Making sense of medical abbreviations
lessons.description: Abbreviations shorten longer phrases.
objectives: Explain making sense of medical abbreviations in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: Abbreviations shorten longer phrases. BP commonly means blood pressure, and HR commonly means heart rate. The surrounding sentence helps establish the intended meaning.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: PO refers to taking something by mouth; IV refers to a vein. These describe different routes and should not be substituted for one another.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: BID means twice daily and PRN means as needed. An abbreviation alone is not a complete personal instruction. Ask a pharmacist to clarify timing, amounts, and any unclear handwriting.

lessons.title: Using medical word parts carefully
lessons.description: Many medical words contain smaller parts.
objectives: Explain using medical word parts carefully in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: Many medical words contain smaller parts. For example, hyper- suggests an excessive amount, hypo- suggests a reduced amount, and -itis describes inflammation.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: Some roots point to body structures: gastr- relates to the stomach, nephr- to the kidney, and derm- to skin. A root can help orient you to a topic.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: Word parts provide clues rather than a complete diagnosis. Read the full definition and context. Similar-looking words do not always describe the same condition.

lessons.title: Understanding blood pressure readings
lessons.description: Blood pressure describes the force of blood against artery walls.
objectives: Explain understanding blood pressure readings in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: Blood pressure describes the force of blood against artery walls. A reading has two numbers and is usually reported in millimeters of mercury, written mmHg.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: Systolic is the upper number, measured when the heart beats. Diastolic is the lower number, measured while the heart relaxes between beats.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: A single number is only part of the picture. Measurement technique and repeated readings matter. Ask your clinician what your readings mean and what target applies to you.

lessons.title: Pulse and other vital signs
lessons.description: Vital signs are basic measurements of body function.
objectives: Explain pulse and other vital signs in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: Vital signs are basic measurements of body function. Common examples include temperature, pulse, breathing rate, and blood pressure.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: Pulse describes the number of heartbeats per minute. Breathing rate describes breaths per minute. These measure different body activities even though both are rates.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: Typical readings vary with age, activity, and health. A reading taken after exercise can differ from one taken at rest. Share the number and its context with your clinician.

lessons.title: Blood glucose in plain language
lessons.description: Glucose is a sugar that provides energy.
objectives: Explain blood glucose in plain language in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: Glucose is a sugar that provides energy. A blood glucose test measures how much of it is in a blood sample at that time.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: Food and test preparation can affect the result. Some glucose tests require fasting, while others are taken at a different time or after a specific drink.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: Check the units and the reference information on your own report. Follow preparation instructions and ask your clinician to interpret the result with your symptoms and medical history.

lessons.title: Understanding an HbA1c result
lessons.description: Hemoglobin is a protein in red blood cells.
objectives: Explain understanding an HbA1c result in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: Hemoglobin is a protein in red blood cells. HbA1c measures the proportion of hemoglobin with glucose attached to it.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: An HbA1c result reflects average blood glucose over roughly the previous three months. It gives a longer view than a single glucose measurement.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: Clinicians use HbA1c to help diagnose or monitor diabetes. Some health conditions can affect its accuracy. Discuss your result and personal goals with your care team.

lessons.title: Understanding cholesterol terms
lessons.description: Cholesterol is a waxy substance used by the body.
objectives: Explain understanding cholesterol terms in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: Cholesterol is a waxy substance used by the body. A lipid panel measures cholesterol-related values and usually triglycerides, another type of fat in blood.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: LDL carries cholesterol toward tissues; excess LDL can contribute to artery buildup. HDL helps carry cholesterol back to the liver. The overall pattern matters.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: Cholesterol results help assess cardiovascular risk alongside age, health history, and other factors. Ask your clinician to explain your report rather than judging one number alone.

lessons.title: Understanding a complete blood count
lessons.description: A complete blood count, or CBC, measures several features of blood.
objectives: Explain understanding a complete blood count in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: A complete blood count, or CBC, measures several features of blood. It includes information about red cells, white cells, and platelets.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: Red cells carry oxygen, white cells participate in immune defense, and platelets help blood clot. Hemoglobin is an oxygen-carrying protein in red cells.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: An unusual CBC result can have many causes. A clinician interprets it alongside symptoms and may request more tests. A flagged number alone does not identify a disease.

lessons.title: What anemia means
lessons.description: Anemia means blood has fewer healthy red blood cells or less hemoglobin than needed to carry oxygen effectively.
objectives: Explain what anemia means in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: Anemia means blood has fewer healthy red blood cells or less hemoglobin than needed to carry oxygen effectively. It can have several different causes.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: Tiredness, weakness, or shortness of breath can occur with anemia, but these symptoms can also have other explanations. Blood tests help clinicians investigate.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: Low iron is one possible cause, not the explanation for every anemia. Treatment depends on the cause, so do not choose supplements based only on the word anemia.

lessons.title: Understanding kidney tests
lessons.description: Kidneys filter waste and extra fluid from blood.
objectives: Explain understanding kidney tests in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: Kidneys filter waste and extra fluid from blood. Blood and urine tests can help assess how well they are doing this work.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: Creatinine is a waste product measured in blood. An estimated glomerular filtration rate, or eGFR, estimates filtering ability. Urine protein tests provide another kind of information.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: Kidney results are interpreted together and over time. A clinician considers age, other health conditions, and medicines. One test cannot explain every aspect of kidney health.

lessons.title: Understanding liver blood tests
lessons.description: A liver panel measures substances related to liver health, including certain enzymes and proteins.
objectives: Explain understanding liver blood tests in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: A liver panel measures substances related to liver health, including certain enzymes and proteins. Different measurements provide different clues.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: ALT and AST are enzymes that may rise when cells are injured. Albumin is a protein made by the liver. These results are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: An abnormal result does not by itself establish a cause or measure all liver function. Medicines and other conditions can influence results. Your clinician may compare tests or request follow-up.

lessons.title: Reading the idea behind a urine test
lessons.description: Urinalysis examines a urine sample.
objectives: Explain reading the idea behind a urine test in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: Urinalysis examines a urine sample. It may assess appearance, chemical measurements, and material seen under a microscope.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: The test can look for clues such as protein, glucose, blood, or signs of infection. These findings can help guide further investigation.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: Collection instructions matter because contamination can affect results. A finding does not always identify a specific disease. Ask your clinician whether a repeat test or another test is needed.

lessons.title: Understanding asthma language
lessons.description: Asthma is a long-term condition involving the airways.
objectives: Explain understanding asthma language in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: Asthma is a long-term condition involving the airways. Inflammation and narrowing can make moving air in and out of the lungs harder.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: Wheezing, coughing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath can occur. Triggers differ between people, and symptoms can change over time.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: An asthma action plan explains a person's medicines and what to do as symptoms change. Follow your own plan and seek urgent help for severe breathing difficulty.

lessons.title: What dehydration means
lessons.description: Dehydration occurs when the body loses more fluid than it takes in.
objectives: Explain what dehydration means in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: Dehydration occurs when the body loses more fluid than it takes in. Illness, heat, or activity can contribute to fluid loss.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: Thirst, dry mouth, and less frequent urination can be clues. Babies, older adults, and people with certain illnesses may be especially vulnerable.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: Severe dehydration can be dangerous. Seek medical advice for concerning symptoms or inability to keep fluids down. People with fluid restrictions should follow their clinician's individual instructions.

lessons.title: Understanding thyroid terms
lessons.description: The thyroid is a gland in the neck that makes hormones.
objectives: Explain understanding thyroid terms in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: The thyroid is a gland in the neck that makes hormones. These hormones influence many body processes, including how the body uses energy.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: Hypothyroidism means the thyroid is not producing enough hormone. Hyperthyroidism means it produces too much. The words describe opposite hormone problems.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: Symptoms can overlap with other illnesses. Blood tests and clinical assessment help establish what is happening. Do not change a thyroid medicine based only on symptoms or a word definition.

lessons.title: Understanding common imaging tests
lessons.description: Diagnostic imaging creates pictures of structures inside the body.
objectives: Explain understanding common imaging tests in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: Diagnostic imaging creates pictures of structures inside the body. Clinicians choose a test based on the question they need to answer.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: X-rays and CT scans use ionizing radiation. Ultrasound uses sound waves. MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves. The methods have different strengths and precautions.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: Tell the imaging team about pregnancy, implants, allergies, or preparation concerns. Ask what the test is intended to show and when to expect a clinician's explanation of the report.

lessons.title: Reference ranges and lab results
lessons.description: A reference range describes results commonly seen in a defined healthy group.
objectives: Explain reference ranges and lab results in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: A reference range describes results commonly seen in a defined healthy group. The range printed on your own lab report is the relevant comparison.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: Different laboratories can use different methods, units, and ranges. A flagged value does not automatically mean disease, and an in-range value does not guarantee good health.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: Positive means the test detected what it was looking for; negative means it did not. Uncertain results may need repeat testing. Your clinician interprets results in context.

lessons.title: Asking useful questions at appointments
lessons.description: Preparing a short list of questions helps you use appointment time well.
objectives: Explain asking useful questions at appointments in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: Preparing a short list of questions helps you use appointment time well. Bring your current medicines and describe the symptoms or concerns that matter most to you.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: Ask what a diagnosis means in everyday words, what each medicine is for, and what follow-up is needed. Tell your clinician when an explanation is difficult to understand.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: Repeat the plan back in your own words to check understanding. Ask for written instructions and whom to contact if a question comes up after the visit.

lessons.title: Preventing medicine mix-ups
lessons.description: A medication error is a preventable mistake in prescribing, supplying, or using a medicine.
objectives: Explain preventing medicine mix-ups in everyday language
Recognize when to ask your care team for clarification

sections.title: The basic idea
sections.content: A medication error is a preventable mistake in prescribing, supplying, or using a medicine. Errors can involve the wrong product, amount, route, or timing.

sections.title: What the words mean
sections.content: Keep a current medicine list and check labels. Share allergies and all prescription, nonprescription, and supplement products with each member of your care team.

sections.title: Using this information
sections.content: If instructions conflict or a product seems unexpected, ask the pharmacist before using it. A reminder app helps keep records, but it cannot resolve an unclear prescription by itself.

flashcards.front: What is an active ingredient?
flashcards.back: The substance in a medicine that produces its effect.

flashcards.front: Where do you find OTC instructions?
flashcards.back: In the directions section of the Drug Facts label.

flashcards.front: What does a generic name identify?
flashcards.back: The active ingredient rather than a company's product name.

flashcards.front: Can a generic tablet look different?
flashcards.back: Yes. Appearance and some inactive ingredients may differ.

flashcards.front: Why learn the purpose of each medicine?
flashcards.back: To understand its intended benefit and discuss questions with your care team.

flashcards.front: Does a medicine being available mean it has no risks?
flashcards.back: No. Medicines can have unwanted effects or interactions.

flashcards.front: Is every side effect an allergy?
flashcards.back: No. An allergy is an immune reaction; many side effects are not.

flashcards.front: What should you record about a suspected reaction?
flashcards.back: The medicine, symptoms, and when they occurred.

flashcards.front: Do antibiotics treat colds caused by viruses?
flashcards.back: No. Antibiotics act against bacteria, not viruses.

flashcards.front: What is antibiotic resistance?
flashcards.back: Bacteria becoming able to survive an antibiotic's effects.

flashcards.front: What is a medicine interaction?
flashcards.back: Something changing how a medicine works or its unwanted effects.

flashcards.front: Should supplements be on your medicine list?
flashcards.back: Yes. Supplements can interact with medicines too.

flashcards.front: What should a medicine list include?
flashcards.back: Medicine names, how much you take, and when you take them.

flashcards.front: When should you mark a dose as taken?
flashcards.back: After actually taking it, so the record matches what happened.

flashcards.front: Why can a bathroom be a poor storage place?
flashcards.back: Heat and moisture may damage medicines.

flashcards.front: Where do special storage requirements appear?
flashcards.back: On the product instructions; ask a pharmacist if unclear.

flashcards.front: What is a preferred way to dispose of unused medicine?
flashcards.back: An appropriate medicine take-back program.

flashcards.front: Should every unwanted medicine be flushed?
flashcards.back: No. Flushing is only appropriate for specific instructed products.

flashcards.front: What does BID commonly mean?
flashcards.back: Twice daily; confirm your own schedule with the pharmacist.

flashcards.front: What does PRN commonly mean?
flashcards.back: As needed; the prescription must also specify how to use it safely.

flashcards.front: What does the suffix -itis describe?
flashcards.back: Inflammation.

flashcards.front: What body structure does nephr- refer to?
flashcards.back: The kidney.

flashcards.front: What is systolic pressure?
flashcards.back: The pressure when the heart beats; usually the upper number.

flashcards.front: What is diastolic pressure?
flashcards.back: The pressure between heartbeats; usually the lower number.

flashcards.front: What does pulse measure?
flashcards.back: Heartbeats per minute.

flashcards.front: Name two vital signs besides pulse.
flashcards.back: Examples include temperature, breathing rate, and blood pressure.

flashcards.front: What does a blood glucose test measure?
flashcards.back: The amount of glucose, a sugar, in the blood.

flashcards.front: Do all blood glucose tests require fasting?
flashcards.back: No. Preparation depends on the specific test ordered.

flashcards.front: What time period does HbA1c roughly reflect?
flashcards.back: Average blood glucose over the previous three months.

flashcards.front: Is HbA1c the same as a single glucose reading?
flashcards.back: No. It reflects a longer-term average rather than one moment.

flashcards.front: What is a lipid panel?
flashcards.back: A blood test reporting cholesterol measures and usually triglycerides.

flashcards.front: Can one cholesterol number describe all heart risk?
flashcards.back: No. Clinicians consider the full results and other risk factors.

flashcards.front: What does CBC stand for?
flashcards.back: Complete blood count.

flashcards.front: What do platelets help with?
flashcards.back: Blood clotting.

flashcards.front: Is all anemia caused by low iron?
flashcards.back: No. There are several causes, and treatment depends on the cause.

flashcards.front: Why can anemia cause tiredness?
flashcards.back: The blood may carry less oxygen to the body's tissues.

flashcards.front: What does eGFR estimate?
flashcards.back: How well the kidneys filter blood.

flashcards.front: Why might both blood and urine be tested?
flashcards.back: They provide different information about kidney function and possible damage.

flashcards.front: What is a liver panel?
flashcards.back: A group of blood tests that provide clues about liver health.

flashcards.front: Does one abnormal liver enzyme identify the cause?
flashcards.back: No. Results need interpretation with other tests and medical history.

flashcards.front: What is urinalysis?
flashcards.back: An examination of urine that can include physical, chemical, and microscopic checks.

flashcards.front: Why follow urine collection instructions?
flashcards.back: To reduce contamination and help make the result useful.

flashcards.front: What part of the body is affected by asthma?
flashcards.back: The airways in the lungs.

flashcards.front: What is an asthma action plan?
flashcards.back: Personal instructions for medicines and what to do when symptoms change.

flashcards.front: What does dehydration mean?
flashcards.back: The body has lost more fluid than it has taken in.

flashcards.front: Can fluid needs be identical for everyone?
flashcards.back: No. Age, illness, and clinician-directed restrictions can change individual needs.

flashcards.front: What is hypothyroidism?
flashcards.back: Too little thyroid hormone production.

flashcards.front: What is hyperthyroidism?
flashcards.back: Too much thyroid hormone production.

flashcards.front: Does ultrasound use x-rays?
flashcards.back: No. Ultrasound uses sound waves.

flashcards.front: Do CT and MRI use the same method?
flashcards.back: No. CT uses x-rays; MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves.

flashcards.front: Does an out-of-range result always mean disease?
flashcards.back: No. Your clinician must consider symptoms, history, and the test context.

flashcards.front: Why use the range on your own report?
flashcards.back: Laboratories can use different methods, units, and reference ranges.

flashcards.front: What can help you prepare for an appointment?
flashcards.back: A current medicine list and a short list of questions or concerns.

flashcards.front: Why repeat a care plan back in your own words?
flashcards.back: To check that you and the clinician understand the same next steps.

flashcards.front: What is a medication error?
flashcards.back: A preventable mistake in prescribing, supplying, or using a medicine.

flashcards.front: What should you do with conflicting medicine instructions?
flashcards.back: Ask the pharmacist or prescriber to clarify before using the medicine.
